articles.title_orig: Trump announces Ukraine energy ceasefire with Russia, surprising Zelenskiy
articles.title_zh: Trump announces Ukraine energy ceasefire with Russia, surprising Zelenskiy
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has announced what he called an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Ukraine and Russia, after mutual attacks on energy infrastructure piled pressure on global energy prices.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed,” Trump wrote on social media on Sunday. “Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios.
But he confirmed Ukraine would back the deal, saying in a post on Telegram: “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side.”
Zelenskyy previously said on Sunday he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day full ceasefire.
On Saturday, Trump slammed the Ukrainian president for attacking Russian oil refineries, the day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were originally imposed to sap Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.
“He better damn well stop,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment , with attacks intensifying in the past few months.
On Saturday, a six-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled her from the wreckage.
In response to Trump’s suggestion of a new leader, Zelenskyy said, “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.content_orig:
United Cajun Navy Incident Cmdr. Josh Gill joins ‘Fox News Live’ as Florida communities begin cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias left widespread damage and power outages in its wake. Gill discusses recovery efforts on the ground and how volunteers are helping residents clear debris and rebuild after the storm.
Communities are beginning to assess the damage left behind by a powerful hurricane that tore through the region, leaving homes damaged, roads flooded and neighborhoods littered with debris.
Photos from some of the hardest-hit areas show the scale of the destruction as residents and emergency crews begin the long process of cleaning up and rebuilding.
HOW THE VIOLENT CATEGORY 2 STORM UNFOLDED ACROSS FLORIDA AND GULF COAST
Copper Brock helps salvage what he can from the Milton Quick Stop after the roof was torn off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Isaias slammed into the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, bringing destructive winds, dangerous storm surge and widespread flooding.
The hurricane tore roofs from buildings, uprooted trees and knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of customers across Florida and Alabama before pushing inland.
STUNNING FOOTAGE CAPTURES HURRICANE ISAIAS FROM INSIDE THE STORM’S EYE
In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
A home is partially destroyed after Hurricane Isaias came ashore. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Alex Dean cleans out his home that was severely damaged during Hurricane Isaias. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Isaias marked the first hurricane to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast since Hurricane Milton battered Florida in October 2024, nearly two years earlier.
The storm also became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, ending an unusually quiet stretch that saw no hurricanes develop until October.
DESANTIS DEPLOYS AN ARMY TO CLEAR ROADS, RESTORE POWER AFTER ISAIAS' LANDFALL
In an aerial view, a worker with Southern Land Services removes a tree that landed on a home when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
In an aerial view, a worker with Southern Land Services removes a tree that landed on a home when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Laura and Alex Dean clean out their home that was severely damaged during Hurricane Isaias. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
As Isaias moved inland and weakened, the full extent of the hurricane's destruction began to emerge.
Stunning images from across the Gulf Coast capture what the powerful storm left behind.

articles.title_orig: Rachel downgraded from 'tropical' storm, but strong winds, rain and flooding hit Southern California
articles.title_zh: Rachel downgraded from 'tropical' storm, but strong winds, rain and flooding hit Southern California
articles.content_orig:
Here’s what you need to know:
Long Beach beachfront home on the verge of collapse
At least one house along the shore in Long Beach appeared severely damaged by the strong waves Sunday morning.
The deck of a yellow ocean-facing house on Seaside Walk along the Peninsula was completely submerged along the side. The impact shattered glass windows and broke wood within the structure as water inundated the home.
The boardwalk in front of the house was destroyed, with only wooden posts remaining standing as waves continued to batter the shore. The house’s balcony disconnected from the walls and hung at a 30-degree angle toward the water.
Two Long Beach Fire Department lifeguards said the house began to collapse on Sunday morning.
The homeowners could not be immediately reached for comment.
Drone footage of the home posted on X by storm chaser Jordan Hall shows the morning high tide battering the balcony as saltwater poured into the structure. The video shows at least three homes that appeared to have taken heavy damage, along with the boardwalk reduced to splinters in some sections.
Rachel may pass, but flooding threats extend until Tuesday, NWS says
The National Weather Service said Sunday that coastal flooding was expected to remain a threat on beaches of San Diego, Orange, Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties through Tuesday.
Newport Beach piers, wedge remain closed as berm appears to hold back the worst
The City of Newport Beach said city beaches remain open, but Newport Pier, Balboa Pier and the Wedge remain temporarily closed due to safety concerns.
The city pleaded with beachgoers to stay off the sand berms built to hold back the onslaught from weekend storms that flooded the community on Friday, noting that climbing on the berms can compromise their structural integrity.
As the worst of the storm appeared to pass, Newport Beach residents breathed a sigh of relief Sunday as the morning’s high tide began to recede.
Along the Balboa Peninsula, streets were dry, and residents walked and rode bicycles along the boardwalk.
Dozers and excavators moved along the beach, reinforcing the several-foot-high berms built to protect homes from the ocean waves.
The scene contrasted with Friday, when high tide surprised the city and residents, flooding Balboa Boulevard and beach homes. Videos shared on social media showed vehicles and homes surrounded by knee-deep water, including those of people kayaking and skimboarding.
Standing barefoot outside his home at 8th Street and Balboa Boulevard, Ross Stewart, 79, held a cup of coffee and stared at the gray sky and the berms.
“I think we’re going to be okay,” he said. “The waves haven’t breached our walls.”
“They were expecting this high tide today to be the worst, and it looks like we’re past it,” he added.
Stewart, who has lived in the beach community since birth, said the city had been working around the clock to build the massive sand berm, the biggest Stewart had seen in years.
“I’d say it’s probably 10 to 12 feet high,” he said, gazing at the wall of sand.
He said his neighborhood last flooded about five years ago. He said the berm and the city’s constant maintenance helped protect homes.
He hopes the city will keep the berm up for the next high tides.
Not far away, a miniature lake formed in the middle of the beach, behind the large berm.
Shauna Parisi, 37 and her husband, Matt Parisi, 37, who live in the area, came out with their three daughters, ages 7, 4 and 18 months.
The couple said the small lake usually appears every four years, but with the recent high tides, this is the third time it’s developed.
“We go with 8th Street Lake,” Matt Parisi said. “It’s the only place that it happens, and everyone comes here.”
“It’s just the topography of this part of the peninsula,” Shauna chimed in. “Usually, you know, if it were a little bit warmer, all the kids would be swimming in it.”
The couple praised the city’s recovery from Friday’s flooding, which happened because the city hadn’t built the large berms.
Staring at it, Shauna said the city was doing a much better job today.
“I thought they were going to build them and then just kind of go away, but they’ve literally been here,” she said.
She said city crews worked as late as 10 p.m. last night and as early as 6:30 this morning.
“I think anytime there’s a little breakthrough, they kind of go back over and push some more sand up,” she said. “We were worried about that today.”
Rachel downgraded from ‘tropical’ storm
Flooding pounds Coachella Valley causing debris flow and road closures
As of Sunday morning, Rachel may be “no longer tropical,” according to the National Weather Service, but plentiful rainfall has caused flooding in parts of the Coachella Valley.
There has been “debris flow” near Palm Desert, said NWS meteorologist Kyle Wheeler.
“Basically, large rocks, mud and debris moving down the side of the mountain into the Palm Desert area,” he said. “This was six miles south of Palm Desert — all these rocks and mud and debris covered the east and westbound lanes of Highway 74 near mile marker 89, south of Palm Desert.”
Roadway flooding has also occurred on the 10 east near Bermuda Dunes, next to Varner Road where the onramp is.
Rainfall reports in the area, Wheeler said, show that the southern portion of the Coachella Valley has been most affected by Rachel’s wrath, including Indio, Palm Desert and areas further south.
By the numbers: the Indio area received 2.13 inches of rain as of Sunday morning. The Jacqueline Cochran Regional Airport and surroundings received 1.72 inches of rain.
Further North, Palm Springs International Airport got 1.17 inches of rain, while Thousand Palms has gotten 1.43 inches.
Wheeler said he expects to hear about more flooding.
“I’m sure there’s been more flooding, but we haven’t had reports of it yet.”
With strong El Niño looming, coastal residents fear Rachel is just the beginning
Suzie Sandoval, 51, owns two houses on 63rd Place in Long Beach that have so far weathered the flooding and waves.
Since Hurricane Marie a month ago, and with the ongoing threat of a record-setting El Niño, she has been preparing for the worst and trying to fortify the two houses.
She has boarded up the first-floor windows, is considering installing hurricane windows, and is having a contractor come out to potentially install a small brick wall to channel water down the alley behind her house.
“We’re just very scared,” Sandoval said, starting to cry. “I’m devastated for my neighbors.”
Sandoval said the seawall needs reinforcement and rocks placed on the shore to break the waves.
Jon Cortez, 65, said he believes his house is probably safe this season, but he’s concerned for his neighbors, as the historic El Niño is expected to bring much worse.
“With the El Niño coming, this is only the beginning, as far as I can say,” he said, watching the track hoe operator shovel sand on top of the ever-growing sand berm.
Cortez blamed the city for not taking permanent measures to keep the ocean from spilling into the streets, such as installing a concrete barrier or reinforcing the sea wall.
“I think it’s going to be a mess,” he said.
Heavy rain cause rockfall between San Bernardino and Lake Arrowhead
The National Weather Service reports rockfall on Highway 18 on a mountainous stretch below Rimforest between San Bernardino and Lake Arrowhead.
NWS meteorologist Casey Oswant said that rainfall in the mountains—0.75 to 1.18 inches over the last 6 hours, with 0.3-0.5 inches per hour— caused rocks to fall onto the road.
The road is not closed. The debris has been cleared, and the road is open.
“It was probably more on the minor side if they were able to clear it that quickly,” Oswant said.
Mexican government discontinues coastal warnings as Rachel weakens
On Sunday morning, the National Hurricane Center said in an advisory that Rachel remained about 255 miles north-northeast of San Diego, moving with maximum sustained winds of 35 miles per hour.

articles.title_orig: Xi Focus: Xi leads efforts toward building Healthy China
articles.title_zh: Xi Focus: Xi leads efforts toward building Healthy China
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- On a small island in the Yangtze River in eastern China, residents don't need to leave the island to see a medical specialist. They can now access modern medical equipment at the township clinic and consult specialists from higher-level hospitals, who pay regular visits to the facility.
In December 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the clinic in Shiye Township, Jiangsu Province, outlining a path for advancing rural healthcare. Shiye is home to five villages and more than 10,000 permanent residents.
"We must shift the focus of healthcare to the community level, channel more medical resources to local communities, and promote equal access to basic public services in urban and rural areas," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission.
This is to provide people with safe, effective, accessible and affordable public health services and basic medical care, and effectively address the difficulties and high costs people face in accessing medical care at the local level, he added.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in late 2012, the Party Central Committee, with Xi at the core, has given strategic priority to ensuring people's health. It made the major decision to advance the Healthy China Initiative nationwide.
From targeted advances in key areas to nationwide coverage of inclusive health services that meet basic needs, China, a country of more than 1.4 billion people, has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development.
Over the years, Xi has visited grassroots medical institutions and households in rural areas across the country, offering targeted guidance tailored to local conditions.
He has focused on preventing people from falling into or returning to poverty because of illness, using remote consultations to help balance medical resources, and addressing healthcare-related issues in rural areas.
Xi has paid close attention to the issues people face in accessing healthcare at the grassroots level and set out clear directions, from establishing five basic systems -- tiered diagnosis and treatment, modern hospital management, universal medical insurance, drug supply security, and comprehensive oversight -- to developing the healthcare workforce and digital infrastructure for smart healthcare.
"We must unswervingly uphold the public welfare nature of the medical and healthcare sector, and not take the path of wholesale marketization and commercialization," Xi said.
He has also called for further deepening the reform of medical and healthcare systems and exploring Chinese solutions to the worldwide challenge of healthcare reform.
Coordinated development and governance of healthcare services, medical insurance and pharmaceuticals have helped reduce out-of-pocket payments to 27.1 percent of total health expenditure.
The vision of ensuring that serious illnesses can be treated within one's province, common illnesses within one's city or county, and everyday ailments at the grassroots level is increasingly becoming a reality.
China has supported the development of 125 national regional medical centers so far, with 75 percent of their hospitals located in central and western regions and other areas where high-quality medical resources are relatively scarce.
More than 90 percent of residents can access nearby medical and healthcare services within 15 minutes. Primary-level medical institutions account for more than 50 percent of all medical visits nationwide.
COMPREHENSIVE LIFECYCLE HEALTH
Xi has also expressed deep concern over the growing prevalence of myopia among students, particularly at younger ages.
The trend, he has said, seriously affects children's health and poses a major issue for the future of the country, and it must be given high priority and not allowed to continue unchecked.
With strengthened efforts to prevent and control myopia among children and adolescents, China's overall student myopia rate declined for five consecutive years from 2021 to 2025, reaching 49.9 percent in 2025, down 3.7 percentage points from 2018.
From enabling older people to enjoy their later years to preventing childhood obesity and myopia, Xi has stressed the importance of safeguarding health across all population groups and throughout the entire lifecycle.
A range of health indicators point to improvements in the country's overall health status.
In 2025, China's average life expectancy rose to 79.25 years, while its major health indicators remained at the leading position among upper-middle-income countries and countries with a population exceeding 100 million. The premature mortality rate from major chronic diseases fell to 13.8 percent, and major infectious diseases and endemic diseases were brought under effective control.
China aims to establish a health system by 2035 that is compatible with a society that has basically achieved modernization.
Xi has emphasized the translation of scientific and technological innovations into practical applications, called for advancing the digital and intelligent development of healthcare nationwide, and encouraged regions with suitable conditions to explore the application of artificial intelligence.
This year, the government work report included biomedicine as an emerging pillar industry for the first time.
In the first half of 2026 alone, China approved 38 innovative drugs for market entry.
China is developing a growing range of homegrown drugs, medical equipment, vaccines, medical consumables and approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
Traditional Chinese medicine is a distinctive component of China's healthcare system. Xi has issued important instructions on multiple occasions, calling for the sector's industrial development and modernization, as well as wider international reach.
China has also continued to deepen health cooperation with countries around the world by promoting the use of artemisinin to benefit patients worldwide, regularly deploying medical teams abroad, establishing overseas traditional Chinese medicine centers, and joining efforts to combat Ebola. Through these efforts, it has worked with other countries to address cross-border public health risks.
Yet as China's economy and society evolve and its demographic landscape changes, people's healthcare needs are becoming increasingly multi-layered and diverse.
"At present and for a period to come, China's health and healthcare work needs to adapt to changing circumstances and refine certain specific policies and measures. However, the path of health and healthcare development with Chinese characteristics must not waver," Xi said. ■

articles.title_zh: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 11, 2026
articles.content_orig:
On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:
Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.
And this week on Face the Nation: President Trump scrambles to cut last- minute deals ahead of the midterms, the latest prompting backlash within his own party. Twenty-three days to go before the votes are counted, and the atypical campaign continues.
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's a good question. The answer? Making sure his loyalists get out and vote Republican. Late Friday, Trump cut a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel in an effort to lower the price of fuel in America.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: He's freeing up a lot of oil for the world, OK? That's a good thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But will Trump's deal with Putin prompt even more Republican candidates to distance themselves from him?
We will ask the number two in the Senate, Wyoming Republican John Barrasso.
Democrats have their own challenges. How are they going to get their loyalists to turn out? We will talk with Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy and the Democratic nominee for Senate in New Hampshire Congressman Chris Pappas.
Then: ICE deportation tactics are back in the spotlight following an ICE- involved shooting in New York City. We will get the latest on that and an update on the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Finally, another view on AI with the chief technology officer at Palantir, Shyam Sankar.
It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.
We've got a lot of politics ahead, but we want to start with a quick update on the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall Friday night and resulted in the deaths of four people.
For that update, we turn to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary.
This is the first Atlantic hurricane of the year, hundreds of thousands of people left without power. I know the president approves some federal support. What is needed?
MARKWAYNE MULLIN (U.S. Homeland Security Secretary): Well, we – we're in touch with the – with all the governors that are affected and might be affected by the continuing storm moving across the nation.
The president has been very involved in this from the get-go. Cam Hamilton, who is our director of FEMA, we started prepositioning assets into every state and working closely with their emergency responders.
Right now, from the conversation I have had with each governor, they're in good shape. We're – we have good partnership. What's interesting about this area is, they're – while they may not have been hit with storms real bad the last two years, they work really, really good together.
When I was talking to Governor Kemp from – you know, from Georgia, he was talking about his relationship with Ron DeSantis. When we're dealing with the other governors, they were talking about how they're cooperating with sending assets to the areas that are affected without power to get the – the power restored.
FEMA is standing by, responding with – with lifesaving responses. The Coast Guard is out in the inner waters and the Mississippi, the mouth of Mississippi, out in the – our shores. And we are still doing some boat rescues, but, really, it's more recovery of the boats, not of the individuals.
So we're working together well as a team. We were – you know, you never can be fully prepared for – for a storm like this, but I can tell you that the coordination from – from the Oval Office with President Trump's leadership to the – to the governors to the county first responders…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … we're all working very closely together.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we hope everyone in that pathway is safe.
I want to ask you about something else on the enforcement side of things. There have been at least 30 DHS officer-involved shootings under the Trump administration, according to CBS's tally of events here. There was this incident last week in New York City.
And the NYPD did release security video that shows a man dressed as a civilian with a gun drawn approaching a car and then punching in the window. I know you have said there were other DHS ICE officers in the area who were put at risk by the driver.
But just to clarify events, when are you going to release the body cameras worn by those officers?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: Well, Margaret, what you're seeing is a pole cam.
What you're not seeing is actual – the audio footage or a different angle, where you have multiple officers that are actually approaching this – this individual named Oscar with a long, very long, extensive rap sheet.
He's only been in the country for – for three years, and he has a rap sheet of four charges of felony robbery, two charges of felony assault, felony larceny, misdemeanor assault, possession of – of weapons, possession of stolen property, two felony charges of drugless – of dangerous drugs, and strong gang affiliation that – that has direct or indirect knowledge of – of a CBP officer that was shot last year.
And this guy evaded officers last month when we tried to get to him.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We knew he was armed. We knew he was dangerous. We knew – or there was a possibility of him being armed. We knew he was dangerous, and we knew he was going to evade.
So when we approached his vehicle, we were giving lawful commands. We had approached him just like any other undercover agency that's out there from local, state, federal or – or county that has undercover officers. We had our badges out, once again, giving lawful demands.
He decided that he was going to accelerate and try to evade again. We had taken every precaution to try to keep that from happening, and – and, unfortunately, this took place.
We would have loved for him to exit the vehicle like we asked him to. He decided not to. And, unfortunately, because of the selfish behavior, he put his 5-year-old at danger. But as far as…
MARGARET BRENNAN: You said they were wearing body cameras. Will…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … the information being released…
MARGARET BRENNAN: When will you release that footage?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: As far – Margaret, as far as the information being released, FBI and HSI is going to do the investigation, continue to do the investigation. When it's completed, we'll release all the information.
There was that 5-year-old you just mentioned. Given that rap sheet and how long you'd been monitoring, how come those officers didn't notice that a child was put in that car?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: Well, what our understanding is, is, he drove into the neighborhood.
We knew his pattern of life, but we didn't know the 5-year-old was in the vehicle. Who did know who the 5 – who was in the vehicle was Oscar. Now, as a father of six individuals – or six kids, I mean…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … no way would I ever put my kids in danger. If I was getting lawful commands – and he knew he was being sought after. He knew the police was looking for him because, like I said, he just evaded a month ago.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: I would have immediately got out of my vehicle to protect my – my – my child.
There's no way I would have been selfish enough to put my child in danger.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: He was absolutely selfish enough to put his child in danger. He's the one that decided to accelerate and – and ram into another vehicle with his 5-year-old in the vehicle, and then tried to accelerate towards other police officers.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: That's – that is – that tells you the type of character that Oscar is. And yet somehow the mayor is out there protesting about this.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: But yet, seven days ago, when an NYPD officer got stabbed in the same neighborhood by – by criminals t

Hurricane Isaias peeled off hotel and condominium rooftops and facades along the Florida Panhandle before charging north Saturday, dishing out torrential rains and the threat of flash floods and tornadoes across the Southeast.
Two people were killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama, and nearly 700,000 customers were without power by midday in four states. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the southern Appalachians.
More than 726,000 people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle have been left without power on Saturday after Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf Coast .
The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply, weakening to a post-tropical cyclone, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.
But residents are bracing for flooding and gusty winds in Isaias’ aftermath as authorities warned of the potential for tornadoes.
The storm is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland as the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still looms for parts of the Florida Panhandle.
It will travel northwards across Alabama and over the Tennessee Valley later on Saturday, according to the National Weather Service.
Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola , police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern US since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump , meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico ’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

articles.title_orig: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.title_zh: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.content_orig:
By agreeing to open Russia’s taps and release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into a starving global market, the Kremlin has achieved something that raw military might on the battlefields of eastern Ukraine could never deliver.
The deal, which involves suspending fuel export sanctions on Russia for six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, will be a welcome boon for a Russian economy that is creaking under the strain of a war in Ukraine that has dragged on far longer than anticipated.
But for Vladimir Putin, Russia’s strongman president, the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue. It is the wedge this deal, and the rhetoric around it, drives right through the heart of the Western alliance, which has aimed to isolate Moscow over it’s war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump spelled out the new and extraordinary reality in stark terms as he mocked the angry reaction of Ukraine’s wartime leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, who derided the deal as a “weak decision by a strong partner” that provides “extra money for this war.”
“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused and he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers,” Trump said before calling for a new Ukrainian leader, essentially blaming high global fuel prices, especially acute in the United States, on Ukraine.
In recent months, relentless Ukrainian drone strikes, flying deep into Russian territory with terrifying precision, have systematically crippled oil refineries that serve as both the economic engine and the fuel tank for Russia’s military.
Amid domestic fuel shortages and severe production cuts, the Kremlin suspended all diesel exports this month so that it had enough for its own needs — a stunning setback for a country that used to be the second-biggest diesel exporter in the world before the Ukraine war.
Whether Russia can actually provide the promised diesel or not, by framing the Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries as an assault on American interests, Washington is effectively aligning its economic priorities with Moscow’s survival — even as analysts have suggested the deal is unlikely to dramatically move the needle on diesel prices.
The US has powerful levers it can pull to get Ukraine to play ball.
Washington no longer provides money and weapons to Kyiv. But vital American intelligence sharing — the digital backbone of Ukrainian defense — risks being cut off if Ukraine now continues to strike at the Russian infrastructure Trump wants left untouched. The threat is real — the US did just that in the wake of the notorious Oval Office blowup last year.
Mindful of the risk , Zelensky has indicated he is willing to cooperate, but only if Russia does the same. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said in a recent statement.
For Ukraine, this entire episode may seem like yet another bitter, existential betrayal by an American leader who has at times acknowledged a begrudging respect for Kyiv’s bold military tactics. Now, its most effective asymmetric weapon — relentless drone strikes on oil refineries — is being undermined and may be neutralized, not by Russian anti-air batteries, but by American diplomatic pressure along with Trump’s irrepressible urge to do a deal with the Kremlin.
In Moscow, on the other hand, the mood is upbeat.
“The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large,” Putin said in an official statement after a prearranged telephone call with Trump on Friday night.
“I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” he added.
Privately, the Kremlin leader must be rubbing his hands with glee.
Both he and Trump want Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries to immediately stop.
Both want Ukraine’s president to be replaced with someone who will agree a quick deal.
And just a few weeks after Trump signed a bill into law, sponsored by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, allowing for punishing sanctions to be imposed on any country that bought Russian oil, Washington has now become a customer itself.
All at once, it seems, a battered but relatively unified Western front that has stood against resource-rich Moscow for more than four years looks like it is being dealt another powerful blow.

articles.title_orig: Catherine Debrunner breaks her own world record at Chicago Marathon
articles.title_zh: Catherine Debrunner breaks her own world record at Chicago Marathon
articles.content_orig:
While attention was focused on the sub-2-hour barrier and the North American record ahead of Sunday’s Bank of America Chicago Marathon, Switzerland’s Catherine Debrunner shocked spectators by breaking her own world record. She flew through the course and set a new women’s wheelchair world record in 1:33:16. Debrunner’s compatriot and fellow world record holder, Marcel Hug , set the course record in 1:21:34 as both Swiss athletes absolutely dominated.
A post shared by Chicago Marathon (@chimarathon)
In the elite running field, Uganda’s Jacob Kiplimo was upset by Kenya’s Amos Kipruto , who won in 2:01:08. Meanwhile, Ethiopia’s Hawi Feysa held off Kenya’s Sharon Lokedi to defend her title in a new PB of 2:13:33. A quintet of Canadian men also lined up to take on the fast course.
From early on, Debrunner and Hug pushed alone on the fast, flat course. Although it’s a quick route, it has many twists and turns that make wheelchair racing hard to navigate at speed. But this didn’t faze Debrunner , who powered through the streets to beat her 2023 Berlin Marathon mark of 1:34:16 by more than a minute.
This was Debrunner’s second straight dominant win in a short time frame, as she also beat Kenya’s Sabastian Sawe in a game of rock-paper-scissors, winning two games to none to determine the order of the London Marathon. In Chicago, she won by nearly nine minutes, with U.S. athlete Tatyana McFadden finishing second in 1:42:01. McFadden was pushed to the line by fellow Swiss athlete Manuela Schär , but won in a photo finish. Schär finished third, also in 1:42:01.
A post shared by Abbott World Marathon Majors (@wmmajors)
Debrunner has been posting fast times in the scene for years, and though her win wasn’t a shock, the world record caught everyone off guard, including her.
“It feels very unreal; I can’t believe I made the world record here in Chicago,” Debrunner told NBC Chicago in a post-race interview. “It has been an amazing day with great weather, and the crowd was great. I didn’t expect to set the world record here, and I’m speechless. I am so blessed to be happy and healthy, and I just wanted to give all I could.”
Swiss compatriot Hug also found a familiar place atop the podium, breaking his own course record and winning by nearly nine minutes. The men’s race mirrored the women’s, with the winner dominating and the second- and third-place finishers decided by a photo finish. Lito Anker of the Netherlands took second in 1:30:11, narrowly beating Great Britain’s David Weir in a photo finish. Weir finished third, in 1:30:11. Josh Cassidy of Barrie, Ont., was the top Canadian and finished 11th, in 01:36:14.
Hug is also the marathon world record holder, setting his mark in Japan in 2021 at 1:17:47. The most dominant wheelchair marathoner of all time has now won Chicago five consecutive years and has now secured his seventh overall victory on the course.
A post shared by Chicago Marathon (@chimarathon)

articles.title_zh: Worthy de Jong named FIBA 3x3 World Tour Bucharest 2026 MVP
articles.content_orig:
Amsterdam's star delivers a dominant all-around performance to lead the Dutch side to back-to-back Bucharest titles.
BUCHAREST (Romania) – Worthy de Jong of Amsterdam RABOBANK (NED) capped a sensational weekend by earning Most Valuable Player (MVP) honors at the FIBA 3x3 World Tour Bucharest 2026 after leading the Dutch side to a successful title defense on October 11.
De Jong was the driving force behind Amsterdam's winning run, delivering when it mattered most as the defending champions won all seven of their games, starting in the Qualifying Draw and finishing with a thrilling 19-17 victory over Fuengirola (ESP) in the Final.
When the pressure peaked, de Jong came through once again. After pouring in 16 points in Amsterdam's Semi-Final win over Miami (USA), he hit the game-winning two-pointer in the Final to seal the title and complete another memorable Bucharest campaign.
Throughout the tournament, de Jong was an unstoppable force, finishing with a tournament-best 58.4 Player Value and 46 points, also leading all players with 26 highlights. He added 20 rebounds, the third-highest total in the competition, and five dunks, ranking second overall.
His all-around excellence helped Amsterdam secure their second FIBA 3x3 World Tour stop win of the 2026 season, following their triumph in WT Vienna .

articles.title_orig: Kelly Clarkson slams New York store for alleged 'Pretty Woman' moment
articles.title_zh: Kelly Clarkson slams New York store for alleged 'Pretty Woman' moment
articles.content_orig:
The Brooklyn shop at the center of controversy over how its staff allegedly mistreated Kelly Clarkson has seemingly offered a thinly-veiled response.
Hours after Clarkson, 44, tweeted about allegedly having a Pretty Woma n-style experience of being shamed over a potential purchase, Art of Play shared a message via its Instagram Story from another customer who praised its staff’s “genuine kindness.”
“From the very first time I walked into @artofplay, I felt welcomed and treated with such genuine kindness,” the review began. “I love discovering unique treasures and connecting with the wonderful people there.”
The customer review went on, “[Art of Play is] a place that leaves you smiling and wanting to come back. I’m already counting down the days until I return in two weeks.”
Art of Play later deleted the customer review from its Instagram Stories.
Earlier on Saturday, Clarkson tweeted about allegedly having a negative interaction with Art of Play’s staff while shopping in the Brooklyn store. (Art of Play sells curiosities and unique toys. It is also a design space and houses a close-up magic theater.)
“Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude,” Clarkson posted.
The Voice coach slammed the offending Art of Play staffer as an “idiot” who’d just lost “a huge sale.”
“But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman . For sure, check it out,” she added.
Clarkson’s nod to Pretty Woma n refers to an iconic sequence from the 1990 comedy, in which Roberts’ escort character Vivian Ward attempts to buy some high-fashion clothing from a Beverly Hills boutique using money from a wealthy businessman ( Richard Gere ) who hired her for a week. A snobby saleswoman ( Dey Young ) put off by Vivian’s midriff-baring minidress kicks her out of the store, assuming she can’t pay for any of the items she wants.
After picking up fancy duds at another store, Vivian returns to the original boutique the following day to give the rude saleswoman a piece of her mind.
“Hi, do you remember me? I was in here yesterday [and] you wouldn’t wait on me,” she quipped. “You work on commission, right? Big mistake. Big. Huge. I have to go shopping now!”
Us reached out to Art of Play for comment on Clarkson’s accusations.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia vows major response after Houthi strike on airport kills 12, injures 309
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia vows major response after Houthi strike on airport kills 12, injures 309
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”
Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title_orig: Mullin says livestreaming Hasan execution aligns with Trump ‘restoring American values’
articles.title_zh: Mullin says livestreaming Hasan execution aligns with Trump ‘restoring American values’
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sunday defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, while saying that he doesn't see an "elevated risk" to U.S. security amid criticism.
"I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime," Mullin said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan ."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last week that the Pentagon planned to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who is set to die by firing squad on Dec. 3 in what will be the first military execution since 1961. The announcement sparked intense criticism , including from some Republicans, like Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who urged the Pentagon to reverse the "gruesome decision," saying there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one."
"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks."
While Mullin defended the Pentagon's move, he said, "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to."
"I follow President Trump. He's the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job," Mullin said. "He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he's restoring America values."
Mullin added that he has "no sympathy" for Hasan, adding, "I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies."
"My job as secretary of homeland security is to protect the homeland, and that's what we do," Mullin said.
The comments come as Vice President JD Vance on Friday cast some doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with the plan, saying he would not tune in if the livestream happens. The vice president said Hasan committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in the attack on the Fort Hood Army base in Texas in 2009.
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Saturday that there are two schools of thought on whether to livestream the execution, saying, "I'll make a decision, ultimately."

articles.title_orig: Democrat Chris Pappas says "we're taking nothing for granted" amid "tough race" in New Hampshire
articles.title_zh: Democrat Chris Pappas says "we're taking nothing for granted" amid "tough race" in New Hampshire
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who's running to represent New Hampshire in the Senate , said on Sunday that "we're taking nothing for granted" as Election Day approaches, amid a "tough race" in the Granite State.
"I'm hopeful about where we're going to end up at the end of this thing, but we've got to put in the work over the next 23 days," Pappas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Pappas, who's represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019, is facing off against former GOP Sen. John Sununu in a race that could be key to determining which party controls the Senate. And although Republicans have been eyeing a possible opportunity to flip the seat, after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced she wouldn't seek reelection, CBS News rates New Hampshire as leaning Democrat.
But Pappas said given New Hampshire's status as a purple state generally and the state's lack of early voting options, his campaign is taking nothing for granted. The focus now is on "how we get to those independent, swing voters, how we energize the base, how we reach out to Republicans over the next 23 days to win a tough race," he said.
Pappas noted that the 2016 Senate race in New Hampshire came down to just over 1,000 votes, and acknowledged how his opponent's family has been dominant in Granite State politics.
"I'm up against a candidate with a very famous political pedigree in New Hampshire. He's been a U.S. senator before," Pappas said. "But this isn't about going back to the failed politicians with failed ideas from the past, it's about looking ahead to the future."
Sununu, the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu, represented New Hampshire in the House and Senate until he lost his reelection bid to Shaheen in 2008. And with a record of breaking with President Trump, he's distanced himself from the president as he campaigns to return to the upper chamber amid an unpopular war with Iran and high gas prices.
But Pappas tied Sununu's campaign to the president's agenda more broadly, and positioned the contest as a larger fight for the Senate majority.
"The fact is, Donald Trump has said this, that 'pretend I'm on the ballot,'" Pappas said. "He's on the ballot through candidates like John Sununu, who will maintain his majority in the U.S. Senate, will make it harder for us to hold this administration to account to address the culture of corruption in Washington and fight to lower costs for New Hampshire families."
Asked about Democrats' priorities should they win control of the House and Senate, Pappas said "we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now."
"We have to put some wins on the board for workers and the middle class," he said. "We can do that by building on the success of the housing bill that we passed to invest in the affordable housing stock that we need, to work to end this war and lower energy prices, to restore the cuts to healthcare that are kicking thousands of Granite Staters off of their health insurance and making it harder for people to access the care that they need."
On immigration enforcement, Pappas has emphasized the need for reforms, while other Democrats have called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be disbanded entirely.
"We have to be realistic — Donald Trump's going to be president for the next two years. We got to find every point of leverage we possibly can to rein in the disgusting abuses we have seen from ICE," Pappas said. "We have to make sure that we are going after the worst of the worst criminals that are violating the law, while also respecting due process rights and making sure that immigrants are part of our extended American family. And people in New Hampshire support that."

articles.title_orig: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.title_zh: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.content_orig:
Imagine a universe where stars still shine, planets still form, and water exists, but liquids are so thick that living cells can barely function. Even with the chemical ingredients for life, the conditions might make living organisms impossible.
Scientists have uncovered a remarkable connection between the fundamental laws of physics and the ability of life to exist. Their findings suggest that even relatively small changes to some of the universe's most basic physical constants could dramatically alter how liquids flow, potentially preventing essential biological processes from taking place.
The discovery, detailed in a study published in Science Advances , came from physicist Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London. His theoretical analysis identified an additional constraint on the values of fundamental physical constants: They must permit liquids to move in ways that support life within and between cells.
The work raises a profound question about the universe. Why do the fundamental laws of nature have values that appear so well suited to the existence of life?
The Fundamental Constants That Shape Our Universe
Fundamental physical constants are numbers that govern how the universe operates. Examples include the mass and electric charge of an electron and the Planck constant, which plays a central role in quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that describes matter and energy at extremely small scales.
These quantities are generally considered universal and unchanging over time. Their values influence everything from the behavior of atoms and chemical bonds to the nuclear reactions that power stars and produce elements essential for life.
Despite their importance, scientists still do not know why these constants have the particular values we observe.
An important clue emerged in 2020 , when Trachenko and his colleagues demonstrated that fundamental physical constants place a lower limit on the viscosity of liquids.
Viscosity describes how strongly a fluid resists flowing. Water has relatively low viscosity and pours easily, while honey and tar are much more viscous and move slowly. The researchers showed that there is a fundamental limit to how freely a fluid can flow, with that limit ultimately connected to the basic constants of nature.
The 2023 study took this connection much further by examining its implications for biology.
Why Tiny Changes to Physics Could Make Life Impossible
Every living cell depends on the movement of molecules. Nutrients must reach the places where they are needed, waste products must be transported away, and countless chemical reactions must occur in a liquid environment.
Another important process is diffusion, the natural spreading of particles through a fluid. Diffusion helps molecules move around cells and enables many of the chemical interactions required for life.
If the viscosity of those fluids changed too much, these processes could become severely disrupted. Liquids that were too thick might prevent vital materials from moving efficiently, while excessively low viscosity could also interfere with the controlled flow necessary for biological functions.
Trachenko explained the surprising connection:
"Understanding how water flows in a cup turns out to be closely related to the grand challenge to figure out fundamental constants. Life processes in and between living cells require motion and it is viscosity that sets the properties of this motion. If fundamental constants change, viscosity would change too impacting life as we know it. For example, if water was as viscous as tar life would not exist in its current form or not exist at all. This applies beyond water, so all life forms using the liquid state to function would be affected."
The implications extend beyond water. Although all known life depends on water, hypothetical organisms elsewhere in the universe might rely on different liquids. The same fundamental physical constraints would still influence how those liquids behave.
Trachenko suggested that the range of constants compatible with cellular life could be surprisingly narrow.
"Any change in fundamental constants including an increase or decrease would be equally bad news for flow and for liquid-based life. We expect the window to be quite narrow: for example, viscosity of our blood would become too thick or too thin for body functioning with only a few per cent change of some fundamental constants such as the Planck constant or electron charge."
These predictions come from theoretical models rather than experiments in which scientists actually changed fundamental constants. The precise limits that different forms of life could tolerate remain uncertain.
A Cosmic Mystery Billions of Years in the Making
What makes the findings especially intriguing is that the same fundamental constants that influence liquid flow also govern the nuclear reactions responsible for creating heavy elements inside stars.
Long before the first living cells appeared, stars were producing elements such as carbon and oxygen that would eventually become essential components of living organisms.
Physicists have long investigated whether the constants governing these nuclear processes must fall within certain ranges for complex matter to exist. But the ability to create life's chemical ingredients does not necessarily guarantee that life can function.
Trachenko's analysis showed that some physical properties governing liquid flow could change without disrupting the combinations of constants needed to produce heavy nuclei in stars.
In other words, a hypothetical universe might still produce the elements necessary for life while having liquids so viscous that cellular processes could not operate.
That means the conditions needed to support life may involve more than the ability to form stars, planets, and complex chemistry. The physical properties of liquids could impose additional requirements on the universe's fundamental constants.
Follow-Up Research Reveals a Surprising Connection to Blood
The investigation continued beyond the original discovery.
In a follow-up study published in January 2025 in The European Physical Journal E , Trachenko and colleagues examined how fundamental physical constants influence more complicated biological fluids, particularly blood.
Unlike water, blood is a complex mixture containing plasma, red blood cells, platelets, and other components. Its viscosity depends not only on molecular properties but also on how these components interact.
For example, red blood cells can form clusters that increase resistance to flow. As the blood moves faster, those clusters can break apart, allowing it to flow more easily. This behavior makes blood considerably more complicated than a simple liquid.
The researchers found something unexpected. Despite the enormous complexity of blood and the relatively large size of red blood cells, its viscosity remains surprisingly close, on a fundamental physical scale, to a theoretical value derived from basic physical constants.
They proposed that interactions between closely spaced blood cells may help explain this connection. Even though red blood cells are vastly larger than atoms, the forces acting where their surfaces approach one another involve distances small enough for molecular and quantum effects to matter.
The 2025 analysis also emphasized an important complication. Estimating which fundamental constants are compatible with life requires accounting for both the intrinsic properties of liquids, determined by fundamental physics, and the additional effects created by interactions among cells and molecules.
These findings offer a more detailed framework for investigating the connection between the universe's basic physical properties and the biological processes that depend on them.
Could the Laws of Physics Have Evolved?
The research also points toward an even deeper mystery: Why do the fundamental constants have values that allow so many different phys

articles.title_zh: SpaceX has a plan to make your phone carrier obsolete
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Space Exploration Technologies (NasdaqGS:SPCX) secured FCC approval for 15,000 additional Starlink satellites, expanding its planned constellation footprint.
The FCC cleared Starlink to operate these satellites without requiring leases of existing ground wireless infrastructure from incumbent carriers.
SpaceX also acquired nationwide 800 MHz spectrum rights, a low band frequency band typically used for wide area mobile coverage.
These spectrum and satellite approvals move SpaceX toward launching Starlink Mobile as a potential nationwide mobile carrier alternative. Our analysis turns up 2 warning signs (1 major) for Space Exploration Technologies as well.
To put SpaceX's Starlink Mobile ambitions in context, explore other companies building the next wave of connectivity infrastructure through 92 AI infrastructure stocks .
Space Exploration Technologies already runs a global satellite broadband operation across the US and multiple international markets, so a move into mobile positions the group directly alongside established telecom carriers. For readers, that means viewing SpaceX less as a pure space venture and more as a full telecom infrastructure player.
2 things going right for Space Exploration Technologies that this headline doesn't cover.
The big Narrative for Space Exploration Technologies is that Starlink and AI infrastructure turn heavy engineering projects into recurring, telecom-like cash flows. Starlink Mobile adds a new test of that idea because it pushes the satellite business straight into the same pockets as AT&T, Verizon and T Mobile.
"Enterprise and government customers are increasing their reliance on secure, low latency satellite connectivity, with SpaceX reporting more than US$6b in new U.S. government contracts in Q2..."
See how the full story points towards a $228 fair value for Space Exploration Technologies .
The FCC approvals and 800 MHz purchase clearly support the bullish Narrative that SpaceX can own both the orbital layer and a slice of terrestrial-style mobile access. Direct to Cell trials with Beeline Kazakhstan already show the model of using Starlink satellites as a seamless extension of phone coverage rather than a separate niche service.
This move also sharpens the main execution risk the Narrative highlights. Turning spectrum and 15,000 extra satellites into a credible nationwide network means heavy capital spend on ground infrastructure, complex roaming deals and tight coordination with Starship launch plans. At the same time, analysts still point to less than one year of cash runway and sizeable quarterly losses.
For any reader, this FCC news only really matters in the context of which SpaceX story you believe: a disciplined telecom-style cash engine or a capital hungry experiment that tests its balance sheet.

articles.title_orig: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
articles.title_zh: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
articles.content_orig:
A man has died after entering a tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and being attacked by one of the animals, police said.
South Yorkshire Police said officers and emergency medical staff were called to Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35pm on Saturday (12:35 GMT) after receiving reports that a man had entered the enclosure.
He died at the scene. It was not immediately clear how he got in.
The tiger was not injured and stayed inside the enclosure during the incident, police said, adding that there was no wider risk to the public.
The park was evacuated, and officers remained at the scene on Saturday night.
“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time,” police said in a statement.
Police also confirmed they were aware of footage circulating on social media that appeared to show the man inside the enclosure shortly before the attack, urging members of the public not to share the distressing video.
Tiger ‘will not be euthanised’
The park said it had closed after a serious incident involving the tiger enclosure and would remain closed until Sunday.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the park said in a statement on its website.
In another statement later on Sunday, the wildlife park offered its “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” to the family of the man who was killed.
“The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” it read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised”.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operating in 2009, and its Land of the Tigers attraction –  a purpose-built 0.4-hectare (2-acre) reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers – opened in 2011.
A raised walkway, 300 metres (985 feet) long, lets visitors watch the tigers roam through woodland and grassland and play in a waterfall pool, the park said.

articles.title_orig: Trump to visit the Philippines next month for ASEAN summit before his second trip to China this year
articles.title_zh: Trump to visit the Philippines next month for ASEAN summit before his second trip to China this year
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump will travel to the Philippines next month for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit before heading on to China, according to the White House.
Trump will participate in the summit in Manila on Nov. 16 before going to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, which will take place from Nov. 17-19, the White House said.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been inviting Trump to visit his country for some time, a US official said.
Trump’s last official trip to the Philippines took place in 2017 when he attended the ASEAN summit. Last year, the president attended the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and APEC in Gyeongju, South Korea, as he works to maintain US influence in Asia.
The president’s goal this year is to demostrate America’s commitment to its allies in Southeast Asia and advance US economic and national security objectives, according to the White House official.
Rumors had been swirling that Trump intended to attend the ASEAN summit this year, but now the White House has officially confirmed it.
Trump will then meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in person for the third time this year. Xi last visited with Trump during a summit at the White House last month.
Trump also met Xi in May in Beijing. The two global superpower leaders are slated to meet in person at the Group of 20 Summit in Miami in December, too.
Both leaders have been working to mend US-Sino relations.
During the summit last month, which marked Xi’s first White House visit since 2015, Washington and Beijing announced various diplomatic initiatives, including an artificial intelligence alert system between the two countries, and Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to China for an education exchange.
In addition, the two sides announced an extension of the nation’s trade truce, which was set to expire next month. It will remain in effect until Jan. 10, 2027, buying two more months for negotiations.
Despite all the pomp and niceties, tensions still remain between both sides.
Talks to date have not appeared to yield any sort of significant breakthrough on Taiwan, though Trump has continued to withhold $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan.
The US is also maintaining key exports controls on China, including for critical technology chips. China has been leveraging its domination of rare earths amid its negotiations with the US on trade.

articles.title_orig: India’s ‘Cockroach’ Leaders Released as Small Protests Go On in Delhi
articles.title_zh: India’s ‘Cockroach’ Leaders Released as Small Protests Go On in Delhi
articles.content_orig:
India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the nation's capital sees demonstrations for a second day, with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.
Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday.
Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated" in his first comments after his release.
Media reports said 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday, with hundreds detained on Sunday.
The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said.
After his release, Dipke posted on X: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India."
He said he was going to his village to attend the funeral of his grandmother, who died around the time of his arrest. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated".
Ranka and Das later told a news conference that the condition did not mean they could not protest.
"Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said.
"Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest.
Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed.
For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded, offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed.
In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there were rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.
Protesters were vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions.
Some were put onto buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants.
Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses.
The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora , who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained.
Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum.
"Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding: "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight."
The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms.
Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue.
At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route.
Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day.
After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday.
On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions.
The court ordered the government to restore the internet, and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there were a disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention.
The row centres on a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide. The commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.
At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms.
Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he wrote on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
Chief Justice Surya Kant says his cockroach comments were misinterpreted.
But Dipke's post went viral and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister.
